notes.b: Every jump in athletics works the same way: the athlete builds up speed in a run-up (the controlled run before the jump) and then turns that speed into height or distance at take-off (the moment the feet leave the ground).
points: Jumping converts the speed of the run-up into height in the high jump, or into horizontal distance in the long jump and triple jump, at take-off. This is why a fast, controlled run-up matters.

The distance or height achieved depends on three things: the take-off speed, the take-off angle (the angle at which the body leaves the ground) and the height of the centre of mass (the balance point of the body) at take-off.
Take-off uses a powerful, extended drive, meaning the hip, knee and ankle all straighten fully, so the jumper pushes for as long as possible against the ground.
The free leg (the leg that is not pushing off) and the arms swing upward at take-off, which adds lift.

Newton's third law (every action has an equal and opposite reaction) explains take-off: the jumper pushes down into the ground, and the ground reaction force (the push of the ground back on the jumper) pushes the jumper up and forward.
notes.tip: Jumps are used as contexts for power, planes and axes, Newton's laws, energy systems (the long jump uses the ATP-PC system) and fitness testing, so be ready to link a jump to these ideas.

notes.b: The Fosbury flop is the technique used to clear a bar in the high jump. It goes through four phases: run-up, take-off, flight and landing. Each one sets up the next.
points: Run-up: the approach is curved and J-shaped, straight at first and then curving in the final strides. The curve is what makes the later body rotation possible.
Run-up: the jumper leans away from the bar on the curve, which sets up the rotation needed to clear the bar.
Take-off: the jumper takes off from the foot further from the bar, driving the knee of the free leg (the leg not pushing off) up to add lift.
Take-off: the body rotates so that the back faces the bar, ready to go over it.
Flight: the jumper arches over the bar with the head and shoulders back and the hips high, then lifts the legs over once the hips have passed.
Landing: the jumper lands on the upper back and shoulders on the mat, which spreads the impact over a safe part of the body.
notes.tip: Remember that the high jumper takes off from the foot further from the bar.

notes.b: The long jump rewards horizontal distance, so the run-up is built for speed and accuracy. The jumper must hit the take-off board without slowing down, then control the body in the air and on landing.
points: Run-up: the jumper accelerates with a consistent number of strides, checked by a check mark on the runway (a marker that lets the jumper confirm the stride pattern), so that the take-off foot meets the board.
Take-off: it is active and flat-footed from the board, without stopping on the board, so that the speed of the run-up is not lost.
Take-off: the free knee is driven up to help the body rotate forward.
Flight: the jumper uses a hang, a sail or a hitch-kick to keep balance and delay the legs dropping, so the legs can be reached forward late.
Landing: the legs are extended forward, and the jumper falls forward or sideways, not backwards, because falling back would shorten the measured jump.
notes.tip: Jumps are used as contexts for energy systems, and the long jump is linked to the ATP-PC system.

notes.b: The triple jump is three linked jumps in one: hop, step and jump. The run-up is the same as in the long jump, but the athlete has to keep speed and balance through three take-offs and landings.
points: Run-up: as for the long jump, the jumper accelerates with a consistent stride pattern.
Take-off (hop): the jumper takes off from the board and lands on the same foot.
Flight (step): the jumper lands on the other foot, keeping the phases balanced.
Landing (jump): the jumper lands in the pit on both feet.
The sequence is always hop, then step, then jump: hop is same foot, step is the other foot, and jump ends on both feet.
The phases should have roughly even rhythm, and speed is maintained through all three, because a weak phase would waste the speed built up in the run-up.
Landings are active and flat-footed, so the jumper can push off again straight away.
Arm action, either single or double (one arm or both arms swinging), drives each phase.
notes.tip: The triple jump sequence is hop (same foot), step (other foot), jump. Do not mix up the order or the feet.

notes.h: Rules and fouls for jumping events
notes.b: Each jumping event has rules that decide whether an attempt counts and how it is measured. Breaking one makes the attempt a failure or a foul.
points: High jump: the take-off must be from one foot.
High jump: three consecutive failures eliminate the jumper, whether at one height or across heights.
High jump: the bar must stay on the supports; knocking it off is a failure.
Long and triple jump: stepping over the take-off board line is a foul, so the jumper must take off before the line.
Long and triple jump: the jump is measured from the take-off line to the nearest mark in the sand made by any part of the body, so a hand or a falling-back landing can cost distance.
Long and triple jump: wind limits apply for records.
notes.tip: In high jump, three consecutive failures eliminate the jumper. In long and triple jump, the measurement runs from the take-off line to the nearest mark in the sand made by any part of the body.

notes.b: An efficient jump is one where nothing wastes the speed built up in the run-up. Most faults come from losing speed or balance somewhere between run-up and landing.
points: An efficient jump has a consistent run-up, speed maintained through take-off, an upright posture at take-off and a controlled landing.
Slowing down before the board is a fault, because it removes the speed that the jump depends on.
Overstriding at take-off lands the foot ahead of the body, which brakes the jump.
Sitting back on landing loses distance, because the measurement is taken from the nearest mark in the sand.
Flattening the curve in the high jump reduces the lean away from the bar and the rotation needed to clear it.

notes.b: Jumpers land hard and take off at speed, so the area has to be checked before anyone jumps.
points: Landing pits are dug and raked before any jump, so the sand is loose and soft.
Landing mats are positioned and checked before the high jump, so the jumper lands on the mat and not on the ground.
The runway is clear of people and equipment during the run-up, so nothing is in the way of a jumper at speed.
Spikes (the studded shoes jumpers wear for grip) are checked for damage before use.
The take-off area is dry, so the jumper does not slip at take-off.

keyTerms.definition: The final push from the ground that launches the jumper into flight, using a powerful extension of the hip, knee and ankle.
The point at which the body's mass is balanced; its height and angle at take-off determine the jump.
The high jump style in which the jumper takes off from the foot further from the bar and clears it back first.
A long jump flight technique in which the legs are cycled to delay them dropping and keep the body balanced.
The first phase of the triple jump, in which the jumper takes off and lands on the same foot.
The second phase of the triple jump, in which the jumper lands on the other foot.
A mark on the runway that a long or triple jumper uses to check that the run-up has the right number of strides.
The board from which the long and triple jumper takes off, over which the jumper must not step.

factCards.term: Triple jump: the order of the phases
factCards.definition: Hop (takes off and lands on the same foot), then step (lands on the other foot), then jump (lands in the pit on both feet).

factCards.term: High jump: which foot to take off from
factCards.definition: The foot further from the bar.
Three consecutive failures eliminate the jumper, whether at one height or across heights.
A hang, a sail or a hitch-kick, used to keep balance and delay the legs dropping.

factCards.term: Long and triple jump: how the jump is measured
factCards.definition: From the take-off line to the nearest mark in the sand made by any part of the body.

questions.prompt: Describe the run-up, take-off, flight and landing in the long jump, giving key technique points for each phase.
questions.model: Run-up: the jumper accelerates with a consistent number of strides, checked by a check mark on the runway, so the foot lands on the board at the right point. Take-off: the jumper makes an active, flat-footed take-off from the board without stopping, driving the free knee up to help rotation and keeping the body upright. Flight: the jumper uses a hang, a sail or a hitch-kick to keep balance and delay the legs dropping, so that the legs can be extended further forward. Landing: the legs are extended forward and the jumper falls forward or sideways, not backwards, so that the mark in the sand is as far from the take-off line as possible.

questions.prompt: Describe the three phases of the triple jump.
questions.model: The triple jump has three phases in a fixed order. The hop is the first phase: the jumper takes off from the board and lands on the same foot. The step is the second phase: the jumper lands on the other foot, keeping the phases balanced and maintaining speed. The jump is the third phase: the jumper lands in the pit on both feet. Arm action, either single or double, drives each phase.
